fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a very simple reason, and it's that it's hard to imagine what this is going to be like until you see it. It's one thing to say, "the AI is going to be very powerful, it's going to do all these things," and it's another thing to actually see it. People don't really react to abstract arguments. They react to what's in front of them.

So let me put it this way. Suppose you had an approach where you build the thing in isolation, in some basement, and then one day you come out and say, "here it is." I used to think there was something appealing about that. But now I think the world would not be ready, and it's not even clear what it would mean for the world to be ready in that scenario. Nobody would have had a chance to adjust. Governments wouldn't have adjusted, companies wouldn't have, people wouldn't have. The gap between what people expect and what is actually there would be too big.

Whereas if the AI is out there, and it's getting better, and people are using it, then something different happens. The concerns stop being hypothetical. If you tell someone "the AI is going to be dangerous" when the AI can barely do anything, it sounds like science fiction. But if the AI is already doing things that make them a little uneasy, then they feel it. I'd say it becomes much easier to care about safety when the capability is visible. And I think this applies to the people who build these systems as well, not just to the public.

So in some sense it's about letting the world see the AI and respond to it, rather than making the response for them.

r001.rationale: The response says it is hard to imagine what powerful AI will be like until people see it, and that abstract arguments do not prompt people to react.

r002.rationale: It presents letting people see and use AI as a way for them to understand its capabilities and respond to them.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict that corporate competitors will collaborate on AI safety.

r004.rationale: It says visible AI can make safety concerns feel real and easier to care about, but does not clearly predict public demand for action.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that it's very hard to imagine something you haven't seen. When people talk about AI that's much more powerful than what exists today, they're talking about something that doesn't exist yet. You can write essays, you can make arguments, but there's a big difference between reading an argument and actually experiencing the thing.

I've noticed this in myself too. Even for people who work on AI every day, it's difficult to feel what the future system will be like. We look at today's models, we see that they make mistakes, they're unreliable in strange ways, and our intuition says, "This is fine, this is a tool." Then you try to reason about a system that's dramatically more capable, and the intuition doesn't follow, even when the reasoning tells you it should.

So if it's so hard to imagine, the best thing you can do is show it. Let people interact with increasingly capable systems so they can update gradually as the capability arrives, rather than all at once. I think that's important for the public, for governments, and frankly for the AI companies themselves.

I also expect behavior to change as AI becomes more visibly powerful. Right now a lot of the discussion about safety feels abstract, so people treat it abstractly. Once the systems start to feel powerful, I think you'll see companies become much more concerned about safety. You may see competitors collaborating on safety in ways that seem unlikely today. Governments will want to get involved. All of that depends on people seeing what's happening, not just being told about it.

There's another part. The world is complicated, and a lot of what we learn about how a system behaves comes from contact with reality. Things you didn't anticipate show up. If you do it incrementally, you have a chance to notice those things, fix them, and build up understanding and institutions along the way. If you only release something at the very end, it all has to be right on the first try, and you've given everyone else no time to adjust. That seems much riskier.

So the thing I've come to believe more strongly is that the gradualness itself is valuable. It's not just a business consideration. It's how society gets to participate in figuring out what to do about this.

r001.rationale: The candidate says essays and arguments differ from actually experiencing a system, and that people struggle to feel what future systems will be like.

r002.rationale: It recommends letting people interact with increasingly capable systems so they can update as capabilities arrive.

r003.rationale: It predicts that as systems feel powerful, companies may become more concerned about safety and competitors may collaborate on it.

r004.rationale: The candidate predicts governments will want to get involved, but does not say visible AI power will generate public demand for action.

fable-5.text:
You know, my thinking on this has changed, and I think it's worth explaining why.

So the earlier view — and it was a view that I held, and I think a lot of people held — was something like this: AI is going to be this momentous, powerful thing, and so the right way to do it is you build it, you work on it, you make it safe, and then at some point, when it's ready, you release it. The powerful AI stays in the lab until you've figured it out. And it seems like a sensible view on the surface.

But I think there are several things wrong with it. The first is that it really underestimates how hard it is to get things right without contact with reality. When you deploy, the world pushes back on you. You discover all these things about your AI that you did not anticipate — ways in which it's not working, ways in which people use it that you didn't expect. The real world is a source of information that you simply cannot replicate inside the lab, no matter how thoughtful you are. And this applies to safety as much as to capability. If you want your AI to be safe, you need to find out how it actually fails, and a lot of that you only learn from deployment.

The second thing — and I think this one may be even more important — is that the abstract idea of powerful AI is very hard for people to take seriously. You can talk about it, you can write essays about it, but it doesn't feel real. When people actually see the AI, when they use it, when it's doing things in front of them — that's when it becomes real. And that's when society, governments, institutions, all the people who need to respond to this technology, actually start to respond. If you imagine the alternative, where the AI is developed in secret and then one day it arrives in the world fully formed, the world is completely unprepared. No one has adapted, no one has built the muscles for dealing with it. That seems much worse.

So you could say the incremental deployment is a way of letting the world and the AI grow together, in some sense. The AI gets exposed to reality and improves from it, and the world gets exposed to the AI and prepares for it. And when you see it that way, releasing in advance, before the AI is maximally powerful, stops looking like a compromise and starts looking like the actual safe path.

r001.rationale: The response says abstract powerful AI is hard for people to take seriously and does not feel real.

r002.rationale: It says seeing and using AI makes it real, addressing the difficulty of grasping AI through abstract discussion.

r003.rationale: The response does not predict that corporate competitors will collaborate on AI safety.

r004.rationale: It predicts that society, governments, and institutions will respond when they see AI, but does not say that public demand will drive action.

opus-5.text:
I think there are two reasons, and they pull in the same direction.

The first one is about us, the builders. It's very difficult to do useful safety work on a system you're only imagining. You can reason about it, and that reasoning is not worthless, but the specific problems that actually show up are almost never the ones you wrote down in advance. You put the thing out, and then you discover that the failure isn't the dramatic one you theorized about — it's something much more mundane and much weirder, and you'd never have found it by thinking. So deployment is, in a sense, how you learn what the problem even is.

The second reason matters more, and it's about everyone else. At some point AI is going to be extremely powerful, and how that goes depends enormously on whether the world has been getting ready. And I've come to believe that readiness isn't really produced by argument. You can explain to people, very carefully, that a system is coming that will be able to do most of what they do, and they will nod, and nothing will change in them. But if they use it, and it's a little bit useful, and then six months later it's noticeably more useful, and then it does something that genuinely surprises them — now they believe it. Now there's a real reaction. Companies restructure, governments start paying attention, people argue about it loudly. That's what you want. You want the arguing to happen while the stakes are still recoverable.

The alternative is a world where the capability arrives mostly as a surprise, and then every decision about it has to be made quickly, by people with no accumulated intuition, under pressure. I don't think that goes well. So the gradualness isn't a concession — it's the actual mechanism by which society gets a say.

r002.rationale: It presents using AI and seeing its usefulness grow as a way for people to grasp capabilities they had difficulty imagining from an explanation alone.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think the main reason is that it's really hard to imagine a very powerful AI. It's hard to feel it. We can talk about it and write essays about it, but it stays abstract. When people finally see the thing, their relationship to it changes.

My view has shifted because I've watched how people react to what's actually in front of them. Before, a lot of the conversation about AI was people reasoning from their imagination. You can't fully do that. The imagination just isn't good enough to extrapolate to something that's genuinely different from anything we've dealt with. But when the AI does something that surprises you, or when it makes a mistake that's strange and revealing, that gets through to people in a way an argument doesn't.

The second part is that I think the right behavior from the companies, the governments, and everyone else will only come when the AI is shown to be powerful. When it's concrete and people can see what it can do, they start to act differently. Companies get more paranoid about safety, governments start to care, and the people building it become more careful, because they feel the weight of it.

There's also the practical point that you learn things by putting systems out into the world that you can't learn any other way. You find the failure modes and you see how the world pushes back. If you build something in secret and drop it all at once, you lose all of that feedback and everyone's reaction is a shock. I'd much rather have it be gradual, so society and the technology can adjust to each other step by step.

So it's not that incremental deployment is a perfect answer, because it has its own problems. But I think it matters a lot that the AI is something people can see and experience as it develops, rather than something they hear about.

r002.rationale: It says that seeing AI do surprising things makes its capabilities concrete in a way imagination alone cannot.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think it comes from watching how these systems behave once people actually use them. From the lab you can imagine the whole arc in the abstract, but you learn much more from putting systems out in the world, seeing where they break, and seeing what surprises people. You can't get those signals from inside a lab.

I'd rather society have time to adapt gradually than be handed something much more capable all at once. People need to build intuitions, norms, and some resilience, and that takes exposure. If we wait until the systems are very powerful before anyone sees them, we lose the chance to learn while the stakes are still manageable.

I hold this with some humility. I'm not confident about how fast things will move, and I don't think anyone should be. But the tradeoff looks clear to me. Deploying incrementally buys feedback and time, and being early and somewhat wrong costs much less than being late and caught off guard.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that it’s very hard to understand something you haven’t experienced. You can talk about what a very powerful AI might do, how it might change the economy, what the risks might be. But when it’s all hypothetical, people can have very different intuitions, and there’s not much to resolve the disagreement.

When people actually experience the technology, that changes. They can see where it’s useful, where it fails, what they should be concerned about. And that includes everyone: the people building it, governments, the broader public. You want there to be time for that learning to happen before the systems become enormously powerful.

Now, incremental deployment doesn’t mean that everything will necessarily go smoothly. There could still be a big jump in capability. But I’ve come to put more weight on the value of giving society experience with what’s coming. We need feedback from reality, and we need time to respond to it.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think there is a limit to how much you can understand something before you’ve actually experienced it. We can talk about very powerful AI, and people can agree that it will be important, but that’s different from seeing what it can do and having it become part of your life.

If you want society to figure out how to deal with AI, society needs something concrete to react to. People need to see the benefits, see the problems, discover where their expectations were wrong. And the people building the systems need that feedback as well. You won’t anticipate everything in advance.

So the argument for incremental deployment is that it gives us an opportunity to learn while the systems are still less powerful and the consequences are more manageable. It gives people time to adapt, and it makes the conversation about what comes next much more grounded. It doesn’t solve the problem of what happens with superintelligence. But I think arriving at that point with some experience is much better than arriving there without it.
